summary: Jessica Warren's October 10, 2023 article argues that the construction industry must improve recycling of construction and demolition (C&D) waste, which the EPA says exceeded 600 million tons in the US in 2021. It lays out ten strategies, including stronger regulation, robotic sorting, deconstruction, material passports, recycled-material markets, training, eco-design, auditing, innovation and industry partnerships. Examples from cities such as San Francisco, Seattle, Austin, Chicago, Denver and Boston illustrate each approach.
one_line: Jessica Warren outlines ten strategies, from regulation to material passports and robotic sorting, to boost recycling of construction and demolition waste.
key_facts: Jessica Warren published the article 'A Blueprint for a Cleaner Build' on October 10, 2023.
C&D waste includes concrete, wood, metals, glass, and plastics, which often end up in landfills.
According to the EPA, the United States generated more than 600 million tons of C&D waste in 2021 alone, a number that has consistently risen.
San Francisco has implemented mandatory C&D recycling ordinances and achieved a recycling rate of 80% for the sector as of late September 2023.
A pilot program in Seattle uses robotic sorting lines to process C&D waste at an unprecedented pace and increase material recovered for recycling.
In Austin, Texas, local construction companies showed that shifting to deconstruction could increase material salvage rates by up to 25% compared to traditional demolition.
Material passports are digital documents detailing the materials used in a building and how to recycle them; they have been piloted in several European countries with success.
A summit in Chicago on November 15, 2023 brought together construction firms, material suppliers, and government agencies to explore an online marketplace for recycled C&D materials.
Denver's local government has provided C&D recycling workshops since late 2023, significantly improving local recycling rates.
The U.S. Green Building Council's LEED certification already encourages eco-design practices that make buildings adaptable to future deconstruction and recycling.
In 2023, firms in Boston began adopting blockchain technology to trace their waste stream and recycling outcomes.
A research team at the University of Florida is investigating recycled concrete as a base for new concrete.
As of late 2023, the National Association of Home Builders has been actively promoting partnerships between waste management companies, construction firms, and recycling specialists.
